I have about 8 mu of good flat land here in Quzhou. I've been farming this plot for decades, and I've learned not to get too clever with it. Around here, the wheat-maize rotation is what keeps families fed. The wheat went into the ground last October—Jimai improved seed, rotary tilled and sown by machine. Right now the wheat is greening up, so my first job is to top-dress it with urea and give it a good irrigation. I'll irrigate three more times before we harvest in early June, and I'll spray for aphids and weeds twice more.

As soon as the wheat comes off, I'll no-till sow hybrid Denghai maize straight into the stubble. Everyone does it this way now—saves diesel, saves time, and the soil doesn't dry out. Maize is easier than wheat: two irrigations is usually enough, and maybe two insecticide sprays plus one herbicide pass. I keep my fertilizer use moderate because the price keeps climbing, but I know what happens if I cut corners—the yield drops fast and the neighbors laugh at you at the grain station.

I thought about cotton because the price per jin is better, but it needs a dozen pesticide sprays and my back isn't what it used to be. Vegetables? Too risky. One bad price day and you lose your shirt. Wheat has the government minimum purchase price, and the maize dealer drives right to the village. It might not make me rich, but it pays the bills and I can sleep at night.
